title: Vietnamese word order
description: Build clear subject–verb–object sentences, add places and combine verbs naturally.
teacher_intro: Welcome to Lesson 11 — Vietnamese Word Order. This is the first lesson in the Sentence Building unit. Set aside about 45–60 minutes. We will use a practical audio-course method: listen to the English explanation, think, speak your Vietnamese answer aloud, then reveal and compare. The central pattern today is Subject + Verb + Object. You will use familiar vocabulary to build complete sentences, add a place, express what you want or like doing, and recognise where question words belong.
background: A basic Vietnamese statement commonly follows Subject–Verb–Object (SVO), much like English: Tôi học tiếng Việt = I study Vietnamese. Vietnamese verbs do not conjugate for person, so học remains học with tôi, bạn or anh ấy. A place phrase commonly follows the main activity in the neutral examples in this lesson: Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà. Verbs such as muốn (want) and thích (like) can be followed directly by another verb phrase: Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt; Tôi thích nghe nhạc. Vietnamese question words often remain in the position of the information they replace: Bạn học gì? (What do you study?), Bạn học ở đâu? (Where do you study?).
culture: The SVO pattern is a useful starting point, but real Vietnamese conversation is flexible. Speakers may omit a subject when it is obvious from context, and a place or time phrase may be moved earlier to establish a setting or add emphasis. Do not treat the beginner pattern as the only possible order. First become confident with complete, neutral sentences; later lessons will show how context, topic and emphasis affect natural speech. In contemporary Hanoi speech, keep the tones clear even when words are linked smoothly.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Welcome to Lesson 11. Today we begin the Sentence Building unit. You already know useful phrases. Now we will learn how Vietnamese arranges those pieces into complete sentences. Set aside about 45–60 minutes. Use the Think, Speak, Reveal, Compare method: hear the prompt, pause, build your answer aloud, then compare.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So today is about the order of the words, not learning a completely new set of vocabulary?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Vietnamese word order is often more familiar than learners expect. A basic statement commonly follows Subject–Verb–Object, just as English does.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Our first model is: Tôi học tiếng Việt. It means 'I study Vietnamese'. Tôi is the subject, học is the verb, and tiếng Việt is the object.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So it is literally I – study – Vietnamese language?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Say each part: tôi… học… tiếng Việt. Now join the three parts smoothly: Tôi học tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: The pattern is: SUBJECT + VERB + OBJECT. In this example, the subject is tôi, the verb is học, and the object is tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Can I change the subject and keep the rest?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Bạn học tiếng Việt means 'You study Vietnamese'. The subject changes from tôi to bạn, while the verb and object stay in place.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: And if I say 'I learn Vietnamese', can I still use học?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Học can mean study or learn. Tôi học tiếng Việt is a natural beginner sentence.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now try a different object. Tôi uống nước means 'I drink water'. Tôi is the subject, uống is the verb, and nước is the object.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi uống nước.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Notice that Vietnamese does not need an extra word corresponding to English 'do' or 'am' here. The verb itself carries the action.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Here is another: Tôi ăn cơm — 'I eat rice' or, more naturally in context, 'I have a meal'. Vietnamese often uses cơm to refer to a meal built around rice.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So the order remains I – eat – rice/meal.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. The order is stable: subject first, action second, object after the action.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's compare two sentences. Tôi đọc sách means 'I read books'. Tôi nghe nhạc means 'I listen to music'. The verbs change, and the objects change, but the basic order stays the same.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Could I say Tôi sách đọc, copying an order I might use in another language?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Not for this ordinary statement. The natural basic order is Tôi đọc sách. Put the verb before the object.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's build the sentence from separate pieces. English prompt: 'I watch television.' The subject is tôi. The verb is xem. The object is ti vi. Put them in that order.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi xem ti vi.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now change the subject: 'He watches television.' Anh ấy xem ti vi. Anh ấy is the subject, xem is the verb, and ti vi is the object.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Does the verb change because the subject is he rather than I?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No. Vietnamese verbs do not conjugate for person in the way English verbs do. Học remains học; xem remains xem. Time and aspect are expressed in other ways, which we will study later.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now let's add a place. Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà means 'I study Vietnamese at home'. The basic subject–verb–object sequence stays together, and the place phrase is added after it.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So I should not put ở nhà before the verb in this sentence?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: For this simple neutral sentence, place it after the activity: Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Try another place phrase. Tôi ăn cơm ở nhà means 'I eat at home'. Again: subject, verb, object, then place.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi ăn cơm ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. A place phrase can also appear earlier for emphasis or to establish the setting, but the pattern we are learning is the safe, neutral starting point.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now we will practise two-verb combinations. Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt means 'I want to study Vietnamese'. Tôi is the subject, muốn means want, and học tiếng Việt is the action you want to do.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: There are two verbs: muốn and học. Do I need 'to' between them?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: No separate word for English 'to' is needed in this pattern. Put the second verb directly after muốn: muốn học.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Another example: Tôi thích nghe nhạc — 'I like listening to music'. Thích is like; nghe is listen; nhạc is music.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi thích nghe nhạc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. The second verb phrase follows the first verb. This is a very useful pattern: subject + thích/muốn + verb phrase.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's compare English and Vietnamese carefully. English says 'I want to drink water'. Vietnamese says Tôi muốn uống nước. The order is I – want – drink – water.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So the Vietnamese sentence is built almost piece by piece in the same order.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. That similarity is helpful, but do not assume every sentence will match English. Learn each pattern as a whole.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now a short question about word order. If the statement is Tôi học tiếng Việt, the question 'What do you study?' can be Bạn học gì? The question word gì occupies the place of the thing being studied.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: So it stays after the verb, where the object would normally go?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Vietnamese question words often remain in the position of the information they replace. You do not have to move gì to the beginning.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Compare: Bạn ăn gì? — 'What do you eat?' The order is you + eat + what. Gì stays after ăn.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn ăn gì?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Now try 'Where do you study?' Bạn học ở đâu? The phrase ở đâu is the place information, so it comes after the verb.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn học ở đâu?

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. We will study question words more deeply in a later lesson. For now, notice the position.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A small but important point: Vietnamese often leaves out a subject when the context makes it obvious. In a conversation, someone might simply say Đang học — 'studying right now' — but we will first practise complete sentences with a clear subject.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: So the full sentence is useful for learning the pattern, even if conversation sometimes leaves pieces out.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Learn the complete structure first. Natural conversation can shorten it once the context is clear.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Let's do a correction drill. I will show an incorrect word order. You say the corrected sentence aloud before the students answer.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Incorrect: Tôi tiếng Việt học. The verb should come before the object. Correct it.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi học tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Correct. Next: Tôi nước uống. Put the verb uống before the object nước.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi uống nước.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Next: Tôi ở nhà học tiếng Việt. For our neutral pattern, place the activity before the place phrase.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Remember, other orders can be used for emphasis, but this is the basic order to use first.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now we will make longer sentences. 'I want to study Vietnamese at home.' Start with tôi muốn, then add học tiếng Việt, then add ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. The structure is subject + want + action/object + place.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: 'I like drinking coffee in the morning.' We have not studied the full time vocabulary yet, but you can recognise the structure: Tôi thích uống cà phê vào buổi sáng.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: The order is still subject, like, drink coffee, then the time phrase.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Yes. Time expressions can move depending on emphasis and context, but this is a clear learner model.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Now a mini-dialogue. Student A asks: Bạn học tiếng Việt ở đâu? Student B answers: Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Bạn học tiếng Việt ở đâu?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Good. Notice how the question and answer share most of the same words. The question replaces the location with ở đâu.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Another mini-dialogue. A asks: Bạn uống gì? B answers: Tôi uống nước.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: Bạn uống gì?

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: Tôi uống nước.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Excellent. The answer places the object after the verb, exactly where gì appeared in the question.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: A Northern pronunciation note: keep the tones clear in học, uống, nước, thích and tiếng Việt. Word order helps the listener understand the sentence, but tones distinguish the words themselves.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt — slow model: Tôi học tiếng Việt. Pause. Bạn học tiếng Việt. Pause. Tôi uống nước. Pause. Tôi ăn cơm ở nhà. Pause. Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt.

dialogue.speaker: NATIVE SPEAKER · NORTHERN VIETNAMESE
dialogue.line: Recording prompt — natural speed: Tôi học tiếng Việt. Bạn học tiếng Việt. Tôi uống nước. Tôi ăn cơm ở nhà. Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt. Tôi thích nghe nhạc.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Listen once without speaking. Listen again and repeat each sentence. On the third pass, cover the Vietnamese text and try to produce each sentence from the English meaning.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I can hear the same basic order in all the examples: who, action, then the thing.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: That is the key. Subject + Verb + Object is your starting point. Add place or time information after the main action in the neutral examples we practised.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Before the final challenge, remember the three patterns: Tôi học tiếng Việt. Tôi muốn học tiếng Việt. Tôi học tiếng Việt ở nhà.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 2
dialogue.line: One action; wanting to do an action; and adding a place.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Exactly. Now complete the practice cards. Say each answer before revealing it. If you make a mistake, identify which part is the subject, verb and object, then rebuild the sentence.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Final speaking challenge: introduce six sentences of your own. Say what you study, eat, drink, read, watch and want to learn. Then add a place to at least two sentences.

dialogue.speaker: STUDENT 1
dialogue.line: I will build each sentence in the same order and check that the verb comes before the object.

dialogue.speaker: TEACHER · ENGLISH
dialogue.line: Well done. You have learned the basic Vietnamese statement pattern. In Lesson 12, we will look more closely at là and identity sentences, and compare them with action sentences.
